name: John Charles Tashner Jr.

roles.title: Radioman, Commander Patrol Wing TWO, Pearl Harbor
Radioman second class, USS Ballard, at Midway
In charge of a maintenance crew detachment, Betio, Tarawa Atoll
Chief radioman, electronics division, fleet plane pool at Majuro

summary: A radioman of Patrol Wing TWO, twenty years old, at Pearl Harbor on the morning of 7 December 1941, and the first participant voice this project holds for that day. Born in Jersey City on 18 December 1920 and raised in Lynchburg, Virginia, by a mother who had left his father when he was three; his service record opens at the Naval Training Station, Norfolk, in October 1938, two months short of his eighteenth birthday, which settles on the later side a tension his family's account carries (enlistment on leaving school at seventeen points at 1938; retirement in 1958 after twenty-one years points at 1937). He served aboard the destroyer USS Selfridge (DD-357) from April 1939, deck force to radio striker to underwater sound operator, and transferred into naval aviation at Pearl Harbor in July 1941 — so the ship the family remembers and the barracks his sons put him in that Sunday morning were never in conflict: by December he belonged to Patrol Wing TWO's communications, maintaining watch of outlying-island and aircraft circuits, not to Selfridge's crew. Both sons say he was mustered out, handed a rifle, and spent the following days recovering bodies from the harbour. From May 1942 he was a radioman second class aboard the seaplane tender USS Ballard, standing radio watches through the Battle of Midway and the search of the battle area; the record credits him with participating in the capture of thirty-six Japanese officers and men from a sunken carrier — Hiryū, whose engineering force Ballard took from an open boat on 19 June 1942 in the Naval Historical Center's account of the rescue. He became an in-flight radio instructor at San Diego, a designated combat aircrewman, made — the record's own words — the invasion landing on Tarawa with CASU-16 and ran a maintenance detachment on Betio, then as a chief radioman headed the electronics division of the fleet plane pool at Majuro, drawing two commendations in 1944. After the war he stayed with aviation electronics through the arrival of airborne radar, flying TBM-3S and TBM-3W aircraft as an operator-technician with anti-submarine squadron VS-22, rated by 1951 as an AEW/ASW operator technician. He refused a commission during the war for reasons his two sons remember differently, married Margaret Monroe Holston — a 1943 San Diego directory has them at 3724 Van Dyke Avenue — retired in 1958 as a chief petty officer with four children to raise, and died in September 1977.

sources.note: the whole shape of the career: Norfolk from October 1938, Selfridge April 1939 – July 1941, VP-23 and Patrol Wing TWO at Pearl Harbor, Ballard at Midway and the thirty-six captured, the combat aircrewman designation, the Tarawa landing and Betio, Majuro and the 1944 commendations, and the postwar run to AEW/ASW.
